doctrines/worship-liturgy/question: How should the Church worship God?
doctrines/worship-liturgy/summary: From Jewish synagogue and table prayers to the Didache, the Divine Liturgy, the Roman Mass, Luther’s German Mass, the Book of Common Prayer, Reformed psalmody, Quaker silence, revivalist new measures, Pentecostal praise and contemporary worship music, Christians have argued over what worship God requires and permits.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/longText:
Christian worship grew out of the Temple and synagogue. Its two poles are the service of the Word (readings, psalms, prayers, preaching) and the Lord’s Supper that Jesus commanded. The Didache’s Jewish-style thanksgivings and Justin Martyr’s account of the Sunday assembly (c.155) show the outline that every ancient rite kept. In the fourth and fifth centuries great regional liturgies took shape: the Byzantine Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac and Armenian rites, the East Syriac Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Roman rite. A Christian year of Easter, Christmas, Lent and the saints’ days grew alongside them. Liturgy was also mission: the Russian Primary Chronicle says the envoys of Kyiv chose Byzantine Christianity because of the beauty of its worship.

The Reformation made worship a battleground. Luther purified the Mass but kept what Scripture did not forbid, the "normative principle", and gave congregations hymns in their own language. Cranmer’s Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1662) gave the English church a single vernacular liturgy. Zwingli, Calvin and the Puritans held that only what God commands may be used, the "regulative principle". They removed images, organs and holy days, and some sang only the Psalms. Trent answered with Pius V’s uniform Roman Missal (1570). Quakers went furthest and abandoned outward forms for silent waiting on the Spirit.

In the modern era Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley made hymn-singing the voice of evangelical piety. Finney’s "new measures" bent worship toward conversion, and Mercersburg theologians and Anglo-Catholics answered with liturgical renewal. The Stone-Campbell movement divided over organs. Azusa Street (1906) launched Pentecostal praise with tongues, dance and spontaneity, and from the 1970s contemporary worship music spread across the globe. Vatican II’s Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963) and the Mass of Paul VI (1969) changed Catholic worship and influenced Protestant liturgies, but they left a traditionalist movement whose standing has swung between Summorum Pontificum (2007) and Traditionis Custodes (2021). Today Ethiopian chant, Korean dawn prayer, African dance and Latin American Pentecostal praise show that the future of Christian worship lies largely in the Global South.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/0/l: How should the Church worship God?
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/0/t: Jesus said the Father seeks those who worship "in spirit and in truth". Should Christian worship follow fixed ancient liturgies or be free and spontaneous? May the church use whatever Scripture does not forbid, or only what it commands? Which songs, instruments, days and seasons belong in worship, and who decides?
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/1/l: Temple, synagogue and psalms (Lev 1–7; Ps 95–100; 150; Neh 8)
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/1/t: Israel worshipped through Temple sacrifice and festivals with priests, Levitical singers, instruments and psalms; after the Exile the synagogue developed reading and exposition of Scripture and prayer. Both shaped Christian worship: the Eucharist as sacrifice and thanksgiving, the service of the Word as synagogue inheritance.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/2/l: "This do in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19–20; 1 Cor 11:23–26; Acts 2:42)
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/2/t: At a Passover-season meal Jesus gives bread and cup as his body and blood; the Jerusalem believers continue "in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers". Every Christian liturgy claims to obey this command.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/3/l: In spirit and truth; psalms, hymns and spiritual songs (John 4:23–24; Col 3:16; 1 Cor 14:26–40)
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/3/t: Paul describes gatherings where "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue", yet insists that "all things be done decently and in order"; believers sing "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs". Liturgical and free-church traditions each claim these texts.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/4/l: Didache: Jewish-rooted thanksgivings and the Lord’s Day (c.100)
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/4/t: The Didache gives eucharistic thanksgivings modelled on Jewish table blessings ("as this broken bread was scattered upon the mountains"), prescribes the Lord’s Prayer three times daily, and directs believers to gather "every Lord’s day" to break bread after confessing their sins.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/5/t: Justin’s description of readings, sermon, prayers, the kiss of peace, offering of bread and wine, the president’s thanksgiving "according to his ability", the people’s Amen and distribution by deacons is the earliest full outline of the eucharistic liturgy.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/6/l: Apostolic Tradition: an early eucharistic prayer (c.215)
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/6/t: A church order ascribed to Hippolytus preserves a eucharistic prayer with thanksgiving, institution narrative, memorial-offering and invocation of the Spirit. Scholars debate its date and attribution, but it shaped 20th-century reforms across traditions.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/7/t: After the Quartodeciman controversy (c.190) over whether Pascha follows the Jewish 14 Nisan or always falls on Sunday, the Council of Nicaea seeks a common Sunday date for Easter, the pivot of the Christian year. Differing calendars still separate Eastern and Western Easter dates.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/8/t: Christmas on 25 December is first attested in Rome (336), Epiphany in the East; Egeria describes Lent, Palm Sunday, Holy Week and the Easter vigil in Jerusalem (c.381–84). Saints’ days and seasons follow, making time itself a re-telling of Christ’s life.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/9/l: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom (c.400 onwards)
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/9/t: Byzantine worship develops around Hagia Sophia: the Little and Great Entrances, the Trisagion, the Cherubic Hymn, the epiclesis and the iconostasis. Liturgy is understood as heaven on earth, participation in the worship of angels.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/10/: Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and East Syriac liturgies (5th–6th c.)

The Oriental Orthodox and the Church of the East preserve distinct rites: the Coptic anaphoras of Basil, Gregory and Cyril; Ethiopia’s many anaphoras in Geʿez with Yared’s chant, drums and sistra; the Syriac Liturgy of St James; the Armenian Badarak; and the ancient East Syriac Anaphora of Addai and Mari.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/11/: Gregory the Great and the Roman rite (c.600)

Tradition credits Gregory with shaping the Roman Canon and the chant that bears his name; historically, "Gregorian" chant emerged from Roman–Frankish fusion under the Carolingians. The Roman rite spreads across Western Europe, displacing Gallican and later Mozarabic uses.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/12/: Beauty that converts: the envoys of Vladimir (987–988)

According to the Russian Primary Chronicle, envoys sent to compare religions reported that in Hagia Sophia they did not know whether they were in heaven or on earth; Vladimir’s Rus’ received baptism in the Byzantine rite (988). Liturgy becomes a means of mission.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/13/: Luther: reform the Mass, keep what is not forbidden (1523–26)

Luther removes the Canon’s language of sacrifice but keeps vestments, candles, chant and the church year, adding congregational chorales. The "normative principle": whatever Scripture does not forbid may be used, if it serves the gospel.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/14/: Cranmer’s English liturgy gives one "common" order for the whole realm: daily Morning and Evening Prayer, Holy Communion, and rites of passage, in "a tongue understanded of the people". It is revised in 1552, 1559 and 1662.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/15/: In Geneva and Scotland the Reformed teach that only what God commands in Scripture may be used in worship: sermons, prayers, metrical psalms, the sacraments. Images, organs, vestments and holy days are removed.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/16/: Trent and the Roman Missal of Pius V (1570)

After Trent, Pius V’s missal imposes a uniform Latin Mass on the Latin Church for four centuries; the Congregation of Rites (1588) polices rubrics. Baroque churches, polyphony and Eucharistic devotion flourish within it.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/17/: Westminster Directory replaces the Prayer Book (1645)
Puritan Parliament abolishes the Prayer Book, replacing it with a directory of rubrics and free prayer and abolishing Christmas and saints’ days. Scotland’s Metrical Psalter (1650) follows.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/18/: Many Scottish and Ulster Presbyterians sing only the inspired Psalms, unaccompanied, holding that God has given the church its hymnbook in Scripture.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/19/: Friends reject set liturgy, sacraments and paid ministry, gathering in silence until someone is moved by the Spirit to speak: worship stripped of every outward form.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/20/: The 1662 Prayer Book and the Great Ejection

At the Restoration the revised Book of Common Prayer is imposed by the Act of Uniformity; about 2,000 ministers who refuse it are ejected, creating English Nonconformity. The 1662 book later travels with the Anglican Communion into Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/21/: Isaac Watts and the Wesleys: the hymn revolution (1707–1780)

Watts’s Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707) and Charles Wesley’s some 6,000 hymns make freely composed hymnody the voice of evangelical worship, though many Reformed congregations resist it for generations.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/22/: Revivalists use protracted meetings, the anxious bench, women praying aloud and direct appeals for decision. Worship becomes oriented toward conversion and measurable results, the root of the altar call and of later "seeker" services.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/23/: J. W. Nevin of Mercersburg argues that revivalism replaces the church’s sacramental and catechetical life with manipulated emotion; Lutheran confessionalists and Anglo-Catholics (the Oxford Movement, from 1833) mount parallel liturgical recoveries.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/24/: Instruments controversy in the Stone-Campbell movement (1860–1906)

When congregations introduce organs, opponents argue that the New Testament shows only singing, and that adding instruments violates the silence of Scripture. The division is formalised when the a cappella Churches of Christ are listed separately in 1906.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/25/: Azusa Street brings spontaneous praise, tongues, prophecy, raised hands, dance, healing prayer and Black gospel music into worship. The charismatic renewal (from 1960) carries this style into Catholic, Anglican and Protestant churches.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/26/: The Council calls for "full, conscious, and active participation", the vernacular, more Scripture and cultural adaptation, the fruit of the Liturgical Movement that had also influenced Lutherans and Anglicans.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/27/: The reformed Roman Missal introduces a three-year lectionary, new eucharistic prayers (Prayer II based on the Apostolic Tradition), prayers of the faithful and vernacular celebration, usually facing the people. Anglican, Lutheran and Methodist rites revised in the 1970s–80s follow similar patterns.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/28/: From the Jesus Movement (Maranatha! Music, 1971), the Vineyard, Integrity’s Hosanna! (1987), Hillsong and Bethel, band-led sets of praise songs projected on screens become the dominant style of evangelical and Pentecostal worship worldwide.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/29/: Traditionalist Catholics and the older Mass (1988–2007)

Archbishop Lefebvre’s unauthorised consecrations (1988) lead to his excommunication and to Ecclesia Dei communities that celebrate the 1962 Missal in union with Rome; Benedict XVI’s Summorum Pontificum (2007) frees it as an "extraordinary form".
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/30/: Critics charge that contemporary worship turns congregations into audiences, favours emotion and individualism over theology, and is shaped by the music industry; defenders reply that every era’s hymns were once contemporary.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/31/: Traditionis Custodes restricts the older Mass (2021)

Pope Francis declares the post-conciliar books the unique expression of the Roman Rite and restricts the 1962 Missal, citing its use to reject Vatican II; traditionalists see a betrayal of Benedict XVI’s settlement.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/32/: African independent churches dance and use indigenous music; Ethiopian services last for hours with chant and drums; Korean churches hold daily dawn prayer meetings; Latin American Pentecostals fill stadiums; Indian Christians adapt bhajans and lyrics. The liturgical centre of gravity moves south.
doctrines/worship-liturgy/flow/nodes/33/: Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches celebrate ancient liturgies largely unchanged; Catholics use the Missal of Paul VI with contested space for the older form; Anglicans and Lutherans keep set liturgies in modern revisions alongside informal services; Reformed and Presbyterian churches range from exclusive psalmody to contemporary bands; Churches of Christ remain a cappella; Quakers divide between unprogrammed and programmed worship; and Pentecostal-charismatic praise is the most widespread style among the world’s 2.6 billion Christians.
